title: 1 Samuel 2:1–10
context: Hannah’s song of praise, kept here as one unit. She exults in the LORD who is holy, weighs actions, brings low and lifts up, guards his faithful ones, and will strengthen his king and exalt his anointed.

verses.text: Hannah prayed, and said, “My heart exults in the LORD! My horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth is enlarged over my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah prays, “My heart exults in the LORD! My horn is exalted in the LORD.” Arminian readers see joyful praise that flows from personal experience of God’s salvation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Hannah rejoicing in God rather than in her circumstances. Readers often compare her song with Mary’s song in Luke 1:46–55, which shares many of its themes.

verses.text: There is no one as holy as the LORD, for there is no one besides you, nor is there any rock like our God.
verses.arminianNotes: She declares, “There is no one as holy as the LORD … nor is there any rock like our God.” Arminian readers see praise for God’s unique holiness and dependable strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God confessed as incomparable. The image of God as a rock appears often in Israel’s worship and expresses his steadfast faithfulness to those who trust him.

verses.text: “Don’t keep talking so exceedingly proudly. Don’t let arrogance come out of your mouth, for the LORD is a God of knowledge. By him actions are weighed.
verses.arminianNotes: Hannah warns, “Don’t keep talking so exceedingly proudly,” because “the LORD is a God of knowledge.” Arminian readers see a warning that God weighs human actions and opposes arrogance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s knowledge exposing pride. The verse turns Hannah’s personal vindication into a wider truth about God’s judgment of the boastful.

verses.text: “The bows of the mighty men are broken. Those who stumbled are armed with strength.
verses.arminianNotes: “The bows of the mighty men are broken. Those who stumbled are armed with strength.” Arminian readers see God reversing human expectations, strengthening the weak who rely on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God overturning worldly power. This shared theme of reversal runs through the whole song and through the story of Samuel, Saul, and David that follows.

verses.text: Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread. Those who were hungry are satisfied. Yes, the barren has borne seven. She who has many children languishes.
verses.arminianNotes: The full hire themselves out, the hungry are satisfied, and “the barren has borne seven.” Arminian readers see God’s compassion for the needy and his attention to Hannah’s own story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God reversing fortunes according to his purpose. The number seven expresses fullness, celebrating God’s complete answer rather than counting Hannah’s children literally.

verses.text: “The LORD kills and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol and brings up.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD kills and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol and brings up.” Arminian readers affirm God’s supreme authority over life and death, which grounds trust in his care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm God’s sovereign rule over life and death. This verse is shared ground on God’s sovereignty; Sheol is the place of the dead.

verses.text: The LORD makes poor and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD makes poor and makes rich. He brings low, he also lifts up.” Arminian readers see God’s rule over human fortunes, which calls for humility in prosperity and hope in poverty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s sovereign hand in raising and humbling. Both traditions confess that God governs human circumstances, though they explain the relation to human choices differently elsewhere.

verses.text: He raises up the poor out of the dust. He lifts up the needy from the dunghill to make them sit with princes and inherit the throne of glory. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s. He has set the world on them.
verses.arminianNotes: “He raises up the poor out of the dust” and seats them “with princes,” for “the pillars of the earth are the LORD’s.” Arminian readers see God’s care for the lowly grounded in his rule over creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s power as Creator securing his exaltation of the humble. This is shared ground: the God who set the world on its pillars lifts the needy according to his good purposes.

verses.text: He will keep the feet of his holy ones, but the wicked will be put to silence in darkness; for no man will prevail by strength.
verses.arminianNotes: “He will keep the feet of his holy ones,” but the wicked will be silenced, “for no man will prevail by strength.” Arminian readers see God guarding those who walk faithfully with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God preserving his holy ones. Readers in both traditions take the line “no man will prevail by strength” as a reminder that security comes from God, not human power.

verses.text: Those who strive with the LORD shall be broken to pieces. He will thunder against them in the sky. “The LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.” Arminian readers see hope for God’s righteous rule through his chosen king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the song anticipate kingship before Israel has a king. Many Christian readers in both traditions see this “anointed” as pointing ultimately toward the Messiah, while also fitting David’s coming reign.
